title: The Last Hour of Pendlewick Workshop
summary: A short cooperative locked-room mystery in a forgotten Victorian clockmaker workshop. A wealthy patron has been found dead beside a stopped astronomical clock, with three suspects, a missing brass gear, and a broken window that may be less helpful than it first appears.

scenes.title: Main Workshop
scenes.description: Dusty benches crowd the warm-lit room. The patron lies near Pendlewick's grand astronomical clock, while the locked front door and silent mechanisms make the workshop feel like a puzzle box.

scenes.title: Display Alcove
scenes.description: Finished clocks gleam in glass cases. Client cards, appointment notes, and an old apprentice drawing make this alcove feel more orderly than the crime scene.

scenes.title: Rear Repair Nook
scenes.description: A cramped repair corner holds spare parts, oil tins, and a narrow ladder. The practical clutter shows who recently moved through the workshop after the lamps were lit.

scenes.title: Broken Window Corner
scenes.description: Cold air seeps through a cracked pane above the alley. The glass, curtain cord, and one carefully guarded folio decide whether the obvious escape route is real or staged.

characters.name: Constable Jonah Reed
characters.description: A steady village constable who keeps the scene calm, notes the order of discoveries, and helps players test whether the locked room was truly locked.

characters.name: Eliza Vane
characters.description: A clever, anxious mechanic who once helped Pendlewick maintain the astronomical clock and resents being treated like a convenient suspect.

characters.name: Crispin Hale
characters.description: A tidy, silver-tongued secretary who speaks carefully about the late patron's affairs and keeps a leather folio close at hand.

characters.name: Nora Bell
characters.description: A practical caretaker with oil-dark sleeves, a tired manner, and a sharp memory for which doors, lamps, and windows were disturbed.

items.name: Patron's Body
items.description: The wealthy patron lies beside the base of the astronomical clock, his evening coat dusted with brass filings.
items.inspectText: There are no signs of a struggle across the room. A small crescent bruise near the temple matches the curve of a clock weight rather than a hand weapon.

items.name: Stopped Astronomical Clock
items.description: Pendlewick's grand clock shows moons, planets, and an alarm dial frozen beneath a dusty glass face.
items.inspectText: The clock stopped at 8:47, exactly where the alarm pin is set. One brass socket in the calendar train is empty, and the alarm hammer is half-released.

items.name: Front Door Latch
items.description: A brass latch on the main workshop door, polished at the handle and scratched near the catch.
items.inspectText: A thin waxy residue clings to the latch notch. Fine parallel scratches suggest a thread was pulled through the gap after the door was shut.

items.name: Appointment Ledger
items.description: A neat ledger of private appointments, invoices, and notes for wealthy clients.
items.inspectText: Tonight's entry names the patron and mentions a private review of 'Hale's accounts before the new trust is signed.' The next line is underlined twice.

items.name: Old Mechanism Blueprint
items.description: A folded apprentice drawing of Pendlewick's astronomical clock, annotated in small, careful handwriting.
items.inspectText: The drawing marks the calendar gear as removable during service. A note says removing it stalls the visible dial without breaking the alarm weight release.

items.name: Narrow Repair Ladder
items.description: A small ladder used to reach the clock's upper panels and the high workshop windows.
items.inspectText: Fresh amber clock oil shines on the third rung. The smear is too high for ordinary floor sweeping and too fresh to be old workshop grime.

items.name: Numbered Parts Tray
items.description: A shallow tray with labeled slots for tiny brass wheels, screws, pins, and gear blanks.
items.inspectText: Slot nineteen is empty and ringed with the same bright oil as the astronomical clock. Its label matches the size stamped on the missing calendar gear socket.

items.name: Broken Window
items.description: A small high window is cracked open above a narrow alley, with glass scattered below the sill.
items.inspectText: One clean footprint in alley dust points away from the workshop. But most of the broken glass lies inside, and the sill dust is barely disturbed.

items.name: Curtain Cord
items.description: A tasseled cord hangs beside the broken window's heavy curtain.
items.inspectText: Tiny glass slivers are caught in the inner fold of the drawn curtain. The pane was broken while the curtain was already closed, from inside the room.

items.name: Secretary's Leather Folio
items.description: A slim leather folio Crispin Hale keeps under one arm, stuffed with patron papers and tied with a ribbon.
items.inspectText: Behind the account papers is a wrapped brass gear stamped with the number nineteen. Its teeth are oily and match the empty socket in Pendlewick's clock.

clues.title: Clock Stopped at the Alarm
clues.content: The astronomical clock stopped at 8:47, the same minute set on the alarm dial, tying the patron's death to the clock's mechanism rather than a random intrusion.

clues.title: Empty Gear Socket
clues.content: A removable brass gear is missing from the calendar train. The empty socket is clean and freshly oiled, so the gear was taken recently.

clues.title: Weight-Shaped Injury
clues.content: The patron's injury matches the rounded edge of a clock weight, supporting a mechanical strike rather than a fistfight or a weapon brought from outside.

clues.title: Thread-Marked Latch
clues.content: Wax residue and scratches on the door latch show it could be set from outside with a fine thread, making the locked room appear sealed after the killer left.

clues.title: Secretary Reported the Lock First
clues.content: Nora did not test the handle herself until after Crispin Hale announced the door was locked, meaning the earliest claim about the locked room came from a suspect.

clues.title: Ledger Threatened the Secretary
clues.content: The patron planned to review Hale's accounts before signing a new trust, giving the secretary a direct reason to fear exposure that very evening.

clues.title: Blueprint Gear Note
clues.content: The missing gear would stall the visible calendar motion but would not prevent the alarm weight from releasing, explaining how the clock could stop while still causing harm.

clues.title: Fresh Oil on the Ladder
clues.content: Fresh clock oil on the ladder suggests someone recently climbed to reach either the clock's upper access panel or the high window.

clues.title: Numbered Gear Slot Empty
clues.content: The workshop's parts tray is missing gear number nineteen, the same size required by the empty socket in the astronomical clock.

clues.title: Convenient Alley Footprint
clues.content: A single clean footprint points away from the broken window, inviting the conclusion that an intruder fled into the alley.

clues.title: Glass in the Drawn Curtain
clues.content: Glass caught inside the drawn curtain proves the window was broken from within after the curtain was closed, making the alley escape a staged false trail.

clues.title: Gear in the Secretary's Folio
clues.content: The missing number nineteen brass gear is hidden in Crispin Hale's folio, still oily and matching the clock's empty socket and the workshop parts tray.

dialogues.question: What do we know before we start touching things?
dialogues.answer: The patron arrived for a private appointment, the alarm bell rang once, and Mr. Hale called for help. He said the door was locked, and the broken window seemed to explain an escape. We should prove each part, not assume it.

dialogues.question: Who first said the workshop door was locked?
dialogues.answer: Mr. Hale did. I was coming from the arcade lamp cupboard when he shouted that the handle would not give. I only tried it after he had already made a great point of saying so.

dialogues.question: Did you hear anything before the alarm?
dialogues.answer: Only the clocks settling and one sharp clack from the big mechanism. Then the alarm bell rang. I did not hear a window break until people were already rushing about.

dialogues.question: Where were you when the alarm rang?
dialogues.answer: In the shuttered arcade, arranging my employer's carriage papers. I heard the alarm, found the workshop locked, and saw the broken window. I never touched that monstrous clock.

dialogues.question: Would a missing gear make you suspect an expert?
dialogues.answer: Not necessarily. Pendlewick labeled the service parts like a schoolroom cupboard. Anyone who could read the tray numbers could remove the right gear if they had seen the clock opened.

dialogues.question: Why was your name underlined in the patron's appointment ledger?
dialogues.answer: Routine bookkeeping. My employer disliked loose ends. It was not an accusation, and I had no reason to fear a review of accounts.

dialogues.question: What does your old blueprint tell us about the alarm?
dialogues.answer: The calendar train and alarm release are separate. Remove the gear, and the face can freeze, but the weighted alarm arm can still drop. The stopped clock is not proof the mechanism was harmless.

dialogues.question: Did you move the repair ladder tonight?
dialogues.answer: No. I sweep floors, not high panels. If there is fresh oil on that rung, someone climbed after the clock was opened, and they were not doing my chores.

dialogues.question: Were you in the repair nook this evening?
dialogues.answer: Certainly not. I would not know one tin of clock oil from another. My business was with papers, not ladders, trays, or greasy little wheels.

dialogues.question: Could the door have been locked after someone left?
dialogues.answer: Yes. With a waxed thread looped around that latch, a person outside could pull it into place and slip the thread away. The room only looked sealed.

dialogues.question: Does the alley footprint prove an intruder escaped?
dialogues.answer: I would not trust it. The alley dust takes prints from anyone passing the arcade. A single tidy mark is too neat, and I saw no trail of glass outside when I first looked.

dialogues.question: You said the broken window explained the escape. How, if the curtain was already drawn?
dialogues.answer: I... only meant it appeared that way at a glance. In the confusion, anyone might mistake glass and a draft for an escape route. I cannot be expected to inspect curtains while my employer lay dead.

dialogues.question: Could the gear in Hale's folio be an innocent spare?
dialogues.answer: No. Number nineteen belongs in that clock or in the numbered tray, not among account papers. And the oil on it is fresh service oil, not old display tarnish.

dialogues.question: What accusation would the evidence support?
dialogues.answer: The fair accusation is that the killer staged the locked room with thread, staged the window to suggest an intruder, used the clock's alarm weight as the means, and hid the missing gear among private papers.

finalLogic.motive: Crispin Hale feared the patron's scheduled review would expose mishandled trust accounts and end his position before the new trust was signed.
finalLogic.method: Hale prepared the astronomical clock so its alarm weight would strike the patron at the appointed minute, removed gear number nineteen to confuse the clock evidence, left the workshop, pulled the door latch shut with waxed thread to create a locked-room illusion, then broke the window from inside during the confusion to suggest an alley intruder. He hid the missing gear in his folio, expecting the staged window to draw attention away from him.
finalLogic.winEnding: The players identify Crispin Hale and explain the full chain: motive in the ledger, mechanical death by the alarm weight, false locking by thread, false escape by broken window, and the missing gear hidden in the secretary's folio. Reed closes the workshop door on a tidy, solved parlor puzzle.
finalLogic.failEnding: The staged window and locked-room claim remain persuasive enough to scatter suspicion among the suspects. Reed keeps the workshop sealed for further inquiry, but the clean solution slips out of reach for now.
